synopsis: NHTSA opened Tesla PE22-002 on 16 February 2022 following 354 unexpected-braking complaints involving about 416,000 vehicles; the case concerned 2021–2022 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles [f11169, f1497]. Complainants described random, sometimes repeated highway-speed deceleration of 10–20 mph over one to three seconds, often in sunny conditions with road shadows [f1498]. By closure on 29 June 2026, the investigation covered 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 incident reports, but identified no crashes, injuries or fatalities and ended without a defect finding or defect action [f1501, f11170, f11171, f1810]. NHTSA concluded that the events neither changed lateral lane positioning nor significantly reduced distance to following vehicles enough to cause a collision, supporting the booklet's conclusion that complaint volume alone does not establish a safety defect [f1503, f1504]. Firmware updates occurred in February and March 2022, and subsequent reports fell to 45 in 2024, 19 in 2025 and three by early 2026; the booklet presents this as evidence that software updates can quickly change the field picture [f1502, f1505]. Its usefulness as a virtual-validation planning precedent is limited: what was validated was not published, and capability-building time, validation time and remaining physical testing were not found [f1807, f1809].
